o: Every word of the shuffled sentence carries its 1-indexed destination as a trailing digit: "is2 sentence4 This1 a3" decodes to "This is a sentence". Reconstruction is pure bookkeeping — read the digit off each word, drop it, and park the stripped word in that slot. With at most 9 words and 200 characters any reasonable method works, but since the positions form a permutation of 1..word-count, a direct bucket fill needs no comparison sort at all. Joining the buckets with single spaces reproduces the original sentence exactly.
k: The trailing character of each word is its 1-indexed slot; strip it after reading it.
Positions are a permutation of 1..word-count, so bucket placement beats sorting.
Words contain only letters besides that final digit, so the last character is always the index.

a.i: Split the sentence into words; for each word, its last character minus one gives the zero-based output slot. Store the word without its digit there and join everything at the end.
s: For each word read int(last char) - 1 as the target index.
Store word without its last character at that index of a result array.
Join the result array with single spaces.
a.t: O(n) — one pass over the n-character sentence

a.i: Sorting the words by their final character places them in order 1..w; strip the digits afterwards and join. Slightly less direct than buckets but a one-liner in most languages.
s: Sort the words comparing their last characters.
Remove the last character from each word.
a.t: O(w log w + n) for w <= 9 words plus n characters — dominated by parsing, not the sort

w: Buckets are the interview answer — they signal you noticed positions form a permutation. Pitfalls: forgetting to strip the digit before joining, letting a stray space survive (split on exactly one space; input has no leading or trailing spaces), and assuming multi-digit positions when constraints cap them at 9. Follow-ups: allow positions beyond 9 (parse the full trailing number), detect missing or duplicated positions, or shuffle rather than unshuffle.
